The panchayat group in Sonpur had two hundred members, and Usha had forwarded the message to all of them: the anganwadi worker, Shabnam didi, was selling the children's ration packets in the next village.

Two days later Rafiq, who drove the school van, stopped her outside the dairy. "Usha, the ration van was late all month. The block office confirmed it. Shabnam didi has been paying for biscuits herself."

Usha's face went hot. Her first thought was, everyone else forwarded it too. She almost said it aloud. Instead she took out her phone right there, deleted the forward and typed a correction in the same group: "What I shared about Shabnam didi was false. I am sorry."

That evening she walked to the anganwadi with her little brother. Shabnam didi listened, arms folded, and then nodded once.

Last term I nearly failed a history paper because a machine sounded sure of itself. I'm Sangeeta, and I asked the AI for three sources on the 1920s textile strikes in Mumbai. It gave me authors, titles, even page numbers, in perfect confident sentences. I copied them straight into my bibliography.

Irfan, a senior who works in the library, glanced at the list. "Which shelf is this one on?" We searched the catalogue. It didn't exist. Neither did the second.

I felt stupid, and then scared, because I had nearly submitted it.

Irfan showed me how to ask the tool for sources and then look each one up myself, in the catalogue or on the publisher's site. Now I treat every smooth answer as a guess until I can check it.

Field supervisor's note, soil project, week 6.

Vishal came in pleased this morning with a report the AI tool had written from his soil test readings. It read beautifully and recommended a fertiliser mix for the farmers' group in Nandgaon. He planned to print copies for the Saturday meeting.

I asked him one question: "Which reading tells you the soil lacks potassium?" He looked at the table for a long time. The tool had used a number from a different sample.

He went quiet and rubbed his neck. I could see he was embarrassed.

We spent the afternoon checking each claim against the raw data, and he phoned the agriculture officer at the block office to confirm the recommendation before anything reached the farmers. He now keeps a column in his notebook titled "checked by me".

On Monday Nour went to the university wellbeing service and joined a Wednesday recovery group. Liam agreed to text her on Saturday evenings. The first slip came two weeks later. This time she wrote down what happened before it.
